transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2026-07-24 11:00 PT / 14:00 ET
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Asha (Horizon Head of Platform), Tom (Cloud Architect), Luis (Security), Nina (PM), Rajesh (DevOps)

Summary:
Quick scoping call for a 2-week POC to validate private networking (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), residency requirements (EU data), and throughput/latency benchmarks. Customer wants no public egress from model hosts, region locking to eu-west-1, and 95th percentile latency <200ms for inference paths. Discussed runbook, benchmark harness, sample payloads, and timeline.

Topics:
- Success criteria for pilot
- Network topo: peering vs privatelink vs transit options
- Egress constraints and allowed destinations
- Workload sizing: QPS, tokens/request, concurrency
- Benchmark plan, metrics, and tooling
- Timeline and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining i think we have about an hour set aside, if folks can introduce themselves real quick that would help.
[00:08] Asha (Horizon): hi i'm asha, head of platform at horizon health, we own infra and platform services for the patient data apps.
[00:14] Tom (Horizon): tom here, cloud architect, i'll be hands on with VPCs and routing.
[00:18] Luis (Horizon): luis, security, focusing on egress, keys, audit.
[00:21] Maya: great, diego and i from redwood will walk through a proposed poc and we want to align on success criteria and constraints. diego over to you for the tech bits.
[00:29] Diego (Redwood SE): thanks maya, quick agenda: network options (peering vs private link), residency and region lock, benchmark goals (qps, tokens), and then a runbook and timeline. also i'll ask for sample payloads to size the run.
[00:42] Rajesh (Horizon): quick note — our legal team requires all model inferences for EU patients to remain in eu-west-1 and no public egress from the serving hosts.
[00:51] Diego: understood, region locking is straightforward in our private deployment model, we can pin nodes to eu-west-1 and restrict routing. on egress — we support both peering and privatelink, but the topology and operational constraints differ.
[01:03] Tom: can you explain the tradeoffs? we currently prefer privatelink to avoid peering across accounts, but we also worry about latency and throughput.
[01:12] Diego: sure. PrivateLink (endpoint services) gives you a managed endpoint and avoids cross-account route table changes, it's simpler for restrictive orgs. peering gives slightly lower hop count typically, so if you're optimizing for sub-100ms tails you might prefer peering. however peering requires VPC route management. for high qps bursts peering + dedicated capacity wins on throughput.
[01:30] Maya: just to add, our Dedicated option provisions reserved GPU pools which are isolated and avoid public NAT egress; for POC customers we can also set up a private control plane inside your VPC (private deployment) depending on contract.
[01:43] Asha: budget wise, we are ok with a short dedicated pilot if the costs are predictable — we need to prove latency and cost per inference.
[01:51] Diego: for sizing, what's your expected qps and tokens? we need average tokens/request, peak concurrency, and SLOs.
[01:58] Nina (Horizon PM): our initial target is 150 qps average for the assistant backend with spikes to 600 qps during peak, average 120 tokens per request, 95th latency target is <200ms, p50 around 60ms.
[02:11] Diego: good details — that maps to sustained token throughput of ~18k tokens/s average and peaks near 72k tokens/s if you're right. we'll need to plan GPU pool sizing: e.g., 8xA100-80GB (or quantized Llama2 style on 4x H100 depending on model) for dedicated to hit those peaks with batching.
[02:29] Tom: are those numbers compatible with privatelink? any egress or throughput throttles on the endpoint?
[02:34] Diego: PrivateLink supports high throughput but the endpoints are within AZ boundaries, you may need multi-AZ endpoints and scaling. Also note that some clouds enforce concurrent connection limits per ENI; we will verify with your cloud account and recommend ENI sizing. for raw throughput peering plus a dedicated deployment yields simpler high throughput behavior.
[02:53] Luis: about egress, legal insisted no direct internet callouts from model hosts. allowed destinations would be our logging/metrics collector (IP ranges), KMS endpoints for key wrapping, and your control plane egress to redwood control plane if needed — though for private we can keep the control plane inside your VPC as well.
[03:10] Diego: we can run the control plane as a private endpoint or inside your VPC, that removes the need for outbound to our public control plane. for KMS, we support customer-managed keys via external KMS/HSM and we can restrict calls to your KMS endpoints.
[03:22] Maya: success criteria you mentioned earlier — let's capture them: 95th percentile latency <200ms for typical assistant prompts, throughput to support 600 qps spikes without queueing beyond 2s, model output fidelity within your eval set baseline, and no data leaving eu-west-1. anything to add?
[03:38] Asha: add audit logging and retention proof for at least 90 days, and SSO access via our SAML provider for the pilot team.
[03:45] Diego: noted, audit logs are supported and we can stream to your SIEM via private connectors, and we have RBAC integrated with SAML.
[03:52] Tom: what's the benchmark plan look like? how long and what metrics will you collect?
[03:56] Diego: propose a two-phase run: phase 1 (day 1-3) is connectivity and baseline: validate peering/privatelink, mount KMS, ensure no public egress. phase 2 (day 4-10) is performance: run controlled benchmark windows that test steady-state qps and burst scenarios with measurements for p50/p95/p99, tail-latency, tokens/sec, GPU util, and cost per 1k tokens. we'll capture token-level traces and KV-cache hit rates if you use prefix caching.
[04:22] Nina: how long do you need sample traffic for the harness?
[04:25] Diego: ideally a small corpus of 1-2k representative requests (we hash and replay them) and a spike generator for the burst tests. we'll also want 5-10 long context requests to validate kv-cache behavior.
[04:36] Rajesh: encryption — do we have support for customer-managed keys for model cache and logs? we can't have logs encrypted with vendor keys.
[04:42] Maya: yes, customer-managed keys for storage and audit logs are possible; we'll enumerate required IAM roles and minimal permissions in the runbook.
[04:48] Tom: if we go with privatelink, what about cross-region data residency? we need to ensure endpoints are strictly in eu-west-1 and nothing falls back to us-east during failover.
[04:57] Diego: we can enforce region routing policies and our runtime supports region pinning; fallback policies can be disabled for the pilot. we'll also add health-check based failovers only to same-region nodes.
[05:07] Asha: ok good. on timing, we want results within 2 weeks so we can present to the board. are the timelines you suggested feasible?
[05:13] Maya: yes, typical 10 business day pilot: 2-3 days for networking & provisioning, then a 3-5 day benchmark window (multiple runs), then 1-2 days of analysis and a recap meeting.
[05:24] Diego: for benchmarks we'll run three main tests: steady-state at 150 qps, burst ramp to 600 qps sustained for 10 minutes, and cache-effectiveness test with repeated prefixes. metrics exported: cpu/gpu util, mem, inferred tokens, cache hit ratio, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and cost per inference.
[05:44] Luis: regarding compliance, can you provide your SOC2 and ISO documents and also a short notes file listing what logs we get and retention?
[05:51] Maya: yes i'll share SOC2 report and a summary security pack. we'll also include a short log schema doc and how to ingest to your SIEM.
[05:58] Nina: what about cost modelling? we need preliminary run-rate estimates for dedicated vs hosted pilot.
[06:02] Maya: we'll produce a cost estimate for a 2-week pilot including reserved capacity options. we'll show per-token cost ranges with and without quantization and with/without KV cache enabled.
[06:12] Tom: one more question — model versions: can we pin a specific model commit and ensure rollbacks?
[06:17] Diego: yes, our deployment supports model version pinning, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to a smaller variant if larger model is unavailable. for the pilot we recommend pinning to a single verified model to keep variability low.
[06:27] Asha: sounds good, next steps then?
[06:30] Maya: recap of next steps: i'll send security pack and runbook links; diego will send benchmark harness template and exact data spec; tom and rajesh will provide sample payloads and egress allowlist; we'll schedule the benchmark window for week of 2026-08-03.
[06:44] Rajesh: i'll compile the egress allowlist and confirm with security by Monday.
[06:47] Asha: thanks all, let's target the follow-up meeting after the benchmark analysis.
[06:52] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in slack and calendar invites. bye.

End of transcript.
